title: Questions for replicate the blood vessel organoid results
body:
Hi,

Thanks for releasing the code and data! I’m trying to replicate the blood vessel organoid results in Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 6 using the provided repositories (Squidiff-main + Squidiff_reproducibility) together with the figshare datasets. I can train the model and generate interpolated pseudo-days, but I can’t reproduce the key figures: the marker trajectories for fibroblast/mural/endothelial cells stay almost flat and the cell-type transitions in Fig. 4e don’t appear.

Could you clarify the missing pieces of the pipeline?

1. Cell-type annotation – Did you release the exact labels used for fibroblast, mural, and endothelial cells in Fig. 4, or the precise marker/thresholding procedure to assign them?
2. Latent interpolation setup – For Fig. 4c–d, which cells did you use to compute the latent direction (only endothelial day 0 vs day 11, or all cell types)? Did you resample latents per cell-type before decoding, or add any noise terms during interpolation?
3. Preprocessing details – How many BVO HVGs were kept, were gene symbols or Ensembl IDs used after filtering, and is there any additional QC (doublet removal, batch correction) that isn’t described in the README?

  Any additional tips or scripts you used to go from the trained checkpoint to the plotted figures would be hugely appreciated. Thanks again for your work!

title: Trouble reproducing Fig. 2 iPSC interpolation (day 0/3 → day 1/2)
body:
Hi, we’re trying to reproduce the iPSC experiment from Fig. 2—training only on day 0 and day 3 cells, then interpolating day 1 and day 2—but we’re not getting the reported behavior.

Because no checkpoint for this setting was provided, we trained our own model from scratch. Below is exactly what we did:

### Data processing

1. Start from the iPSC dataset referenced in the paper (Zenodo record 3625024).
2. Filter cells to keep only day 0–day 3 samples, remove low-quality cells (total counts ≥ 1,000; 200 ≤ genes expressed ≤ 8,000; mitochondrial fraction ≤ 20%).
3. Normalize per cell to 1 × 10⁴ counts, log1p transform.
4. Select 203 highly variable genes (as described in the paper) and force-include the marker genes mentioned around Fig. 2 (NANOG, T, GATA6, POU5F1, HAND1, MKI67, ETV2, CLDN5, PECAM1, SOX17, COL4A1, DCN, ACTA2, PDGFRB, FOXA2, EOMES, MIXL1, COL5A1, CXCR4, NR2F2, GJA4, PGF, RGS16, ADAMTS18).
5. Training data: random balanced sample of 1,200 cells from day 0 and 1,200 cells from day 3 (so only day 0/3 go into training).
6. Evaluation data: separate balanced sample of 600 cells per day across day 0–3 (used purely for interpolation/evaluation).

### Training configuration

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2 python train_squidiff.py \
       --logger_path logs/ipsc_fig2_run \
       --resume_checkpoint checkpoints/ipsc_fig2_run \
       --data_path datasets/ipsc_fig2_train.h5ad \
       --gene_size 203 \
       --output_dim 203 \
       --num_layers 3 \
       --batch_size 64 \
       --microbatch -1 \
       --lr 1e-4 \
       --diffusion_steps 1000 \
       --lr_anneal_steps 100000 \
       --log_interval 200 \
       --save_interval 2000 \
       --use_drug_structure False

Training with loss ≈ 0.03, and gradients looked stable.

### Evaluation procedure

- Encode the evaluation split (day 0–3), treat Group 0 as “start” (day 0) and Group 3 as “target” (day 3).
- Compute Δz in the semantic latent space and interpolate at fractions corresponding to days 1 and 2.
- Generate 1,000 cells per interpolated day and compare to the held-out real day 1/2 cells:
      - UMAP overlay (real vs generated)
      - Mean-expression scatter
      - Flattened Pearson/R²/MAE/RMSE.

### Observed results

For both day 1 and day 2 comparisons we get:

- Mean-level Pearson ≈ 0.17, R² ≈ –0.04
- Flattened R² ≈ –0.06, RMSE ≈ 0.58, MAE ≈ 0.30
- UMAPs show almost no overlap between real and generated cells; the model behaves like a noisy baseline rather than capturing the day 1/2 state.

### Paper reference

Fig. 2b–c and Supplementary Fig. 2 report that Squidiff, trained only on days 0 and 3, “accurately predicts single-cell transcriptomics from day 1 to day 3,” showing smooth differentiation trajectories. We aren’t seeing that behavior—the interpolated cells stay far from the real day 1/2 distribution.

### Questions

1. Are we missing any preprocessing steps (e.g., scaling, gene ordering, semantic-encoder options) that were crucial in your Fig. 2 notebook?
2. Do the iPSC experiments use different architecture settings (gene_size/output_dim, num_layers, channels, EMA, etc.) or training tricks (e.g., curriculum, lower LR) that we should replicate?
3. Is the new Figshare checkpoint (“VO_diff_model.pt”) intended for this iPSC interpolation, or is there a separate checkpoint for Fig. 2 that we should request?
4. Any guidance on diagnosing why our R² stays negative despite following the published description?

Thanks in advance for pointing out what we’re missing—we’d love to line up our replication with the paper’s results.

title: Squidiff as a training framework vs pretrained model
body:
I'm looking for a pretrained model that I can use to generate the perturbed cell state in response to genetic/chemical perturbations, and I came across Squidiff. 

I just wanted to confirm whether Squidiff is i) a training framework that I need to use to train models using my dataset(s), or ii) something that offers pretrained models that I can either use directly (zero-shot) or after minimal fine-tuning for predictions on my datasets. 

Based on my understanding, it is the former, but I'd appreciate it if you could confirm.

title: Question about the choice of input data (log-normalized) for the diffusion model
body:
Dear Author,

Hello! I have read your paper with great interest. As a newcomer to this field, I have a few questions regarding some details that were not mentioned in this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tmyuSya_hUM&t=931s):

① After preprocessing gene and cell filtering, it seems you used log-normalized data (all positive values) as input. I have reviewed some related literature, such as scFoundation and STATE, which use raw counts as input, while other models use scaled data (resulting in both positive and negative values). Could you share the reasoning behind your choice of input data?

② Diffusion models are indeed a milestone in generative models, but DDPM was originally designed for images (grayscale or RGB, where values are typically constrained to [-1,1] or [0,1]). Do biological expression data require additional normalization or scaling before being fed into the model?

③ Since log-normalized data is used as input, you mentioned in the method section that the semantic encoder uses ReLU, while the diffusion model uses SiLU. To my knowledge, SiLU does not guarantee non-negative outputs like ReLU does. When I trained the diffusion model with the same input for 200 epochs, the predicted results from the saved .pt file contained negative values and were unrealistically scaled. Could you provide some insights into this?

I would greatly appreciate your response. Thank you for your time and contribution to the field!

title: Cell number requirements for training Squidiff on time-series scRNA-seq data
body:
Hello, thank you for releasing Squidiff—this is a very interesting and useful framework.

I have a question regarding the cell number requirements for model training. In particular:

If expression data from an initial time point and an intermediate time point are used as inputs, and the goal is to predict the expression matrix of a missing/intermediate state, approximately how many cells are typically required?

Is there a recommended minimum number of cells per time point for stable training and inference?

title: Question regarding the number and selection strategy of highly variable genes in Squidiff training
body:
Dear Author,

Hello！Thank you for the detailed work on Squidiff. I was reviewing the description of the training tasks and have a question about the iPSC differentiation prediction task.

The description states: "we selected the top 203 most variable genes, balancing biological significance with computational efficiency."

Could you please elaborate on the following points?

1. **​Specific Number 203**:​​ What was the rationale behind selecting exactly ​203​ genes?
2. **​Selection Strategy**:​​ You mention balancing biological significance with computational efficiency. Could you detail the ​exact criteria and steps​ used for selecting these top variable genes
3. ​**Model Requirement on Gene Count**:​​ I noticed that other tasks mentioned  also seem to use around 200 genes. Does the Squidiff model architecture or training framework have a ​specific requirement or strong preference for an input gene number in this range​? 

Understanding the reasoning behind these design choices would be very helpful for applying and interpreting the model.

Thank you for your time and clarification.

body:
Dear authors,

Congratulations of the publication of your paper! 

I have a question regarding Figure 3I, where you benchmark squidiff agains PRNet on sciplex3. I couldn't find any code related to the training of PRNet (not here, nor in the other reproducibility repo). Was PRNet trained on the same preprocessed dataset as the one used for squidiff? title: Another perspective on Squidiff's latent space
body:
Title: Another perspective on Squidiff's latent space

    Hi Siyu and team,

    Great work on Squidiff! I read your paper with great interest.

    I have a different perspective that might be relevant: I've been working on a frequency-based framework called 369. From this viewpoint, Squidiff's latent space is essentially a frequency manifold where cell states, perturbations, and differentiation directions correspond to different frequency layers.

    I wrote a short article expanding on this (in Chinese):
    https://369.fyi/insight/squidiff-369.html

    Just sharing in case it sparks any ideas. Would love to hear your thoughts.

    Best,
    Zuo En
